newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy pulls out all the stops to meet EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy pulls out all the stops to meet EMU.

text.p: Italy is determined to be among the first wave of countries into a single European currency, and even if it is using creative accounting to meet tough budgetary goals, the markets love it, analysts said on Friday.

In an 11th hour scramble to get the country into shape for the planned launch of economic and monetary union (EMU), Prime Minister Romano Prodi is preparing to introduce a special "Euro- tax" as well as shift funds from asset sales to cut the deficit.

The government says these and other measures should enable Italy to reduce the ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent in 1997, the magic figure states must meet to make the grade for the launch of the EMU in 1999.
"1997 is basically the 'f' year, where 'f' stands for fudge," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London.
"Everyone around Europe is fudging their deficit targets... the markets know this but if Italy can arithmetically get to the three percent target they are going to be in near nirvana."
Italian financial markets surged on Friday after early details of the budget ignited optimism that the package might be enough to get Italy on the first boat to EMU.
Among the measures planned for next year is a special one-off hike across a range of taxes which is expected to bring in 12.5 trillion lire ($8.2 billion).

The Maastricht Treaty calls on governments to introduce structural budget changes to get their economies into shape, but analysts said the European Commission would not be worried by the apparent short-term nature of the so-called "Euro-tax".
"We all know that in Italy tax increases that start off as temporary soon become permanent," said Giovanna Mossetti, chief economist at Milan brokers Caboto.

The government said it would also raise 12.5 trillion lire from as yet undefined "treasury operations" and was hoping to divert funds from the forthcoming sales of energy giant ENI and electricity utility Enel towards cutting the deficit.

At present under Italian law, money raised by privatisations can only be used to reduce the debt mountain and not the annual budget deficit, but Prodi has been impressed by French plans to use a whopping 37.5 billion francs ($7.4 billion) in its budget accounts next year from the planned sale of France Telecom.
The European Commission has yet to rule on the French move, but if it is accepted, Italy will follow suite.
"Anything the French can do with fudging, Italy can do better," Mossetti said.
However all these measures may still not be enough to cut in half Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio to three percent in 1997 from the expected 6.09 percent this year.
Corriere della Sera wrote on Friday that there were rumours the Treasury might try some window-dressing to redefine the term 'GDP', but it would have its work cut out.
At present, the government is already using a restricted definition of the deficit-to-GDP ratio.
The Maastricht Treaty refers to another, broader definition of the ratio, which in Italy is running some one percentage point higher than the officially quoted figure.

This means that even if Italy reaches its three percent target it would not meet Brussels standards. But analysts say markets are not unduly concerned, hoping that Italy will have shown enough goodwill to win its place in EMU.

"The (budget) is probably insufficient to meet the Maastricht criteria, and will definitely be so if the definition of borrowing requirement according to EU standards is considered, but the political signal is extremely strong," Bank of America wrote in a note to clients on Friday.
